title: Almost persuaded (Acts 25–26)
hookLine: before King Agrippa, Paul: I would that you were as I am, except these chains
tomorrow: fourteen days, no sun, no stars. who gives the pep talk?

cards: Some people hear your whole story and say, that's a lot, maybe later. Paul has heard that before.

Now he's brought out before a king, and Acts brings the room in with great pomp: King Agrippa and Bernice, the chief captains, the principal men of the city. The governor, Festus, has a prisoner he can't explain.
The king says, "Thou art permitted to speak for thyself." Paul stretches out his hand and tells it all again: the road, the light, the voice. Halfway through, the governor cuts in.

teach.b: Festus shouts, "Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad." Paul stays calm: "I am not mad, most noble Festus; but speak forth the words of truth and soberness." Then he turns to the king.
You know these things, he says, "for this thing was not done in a corner."
And Agrippa answers with the line this day is named for: "Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian." Some readers hear a king nearly won over.
Others hear a dry brush-off: you think you'll make me a Christian that fast? Acts doesn't say which.
What it keeps is Paul's reply: "I would to God, that not only thou, but also all that hear me this day, were both almost, and altogether such as I am, except these bonds."
He wishes them everything he has: the hope, the road, the light.
Everything except the chains on his own wrists.
No last argument. A wish, said out loud, and left there. Then the king rises, the room empties, and away from the crowd the officials agree: "This man doeth nothing worthy of death or of bonds."

how: Acts 26 is one of the places where Paul tells his story again; some Christians pray for family and friends by name and leave the rest with God, without pressing them.

games.q: your cousin hears you talk about something that changed you and says, 'almost, but not for me.' what does Paul's answer to Agrippa model?
o: give one more argument while you still have her attention.
wish her every good thing, say so, and leave it there.
drop it, and quietly decide she isn't open to anything.
games.why: Paul doesn't press the king again. he says what he wishes for him, everything except the chains, and the room empties.

practice: Take a scrap of paper. Write one person's name, and under it one good thing you'd wish for them, the way Paul wished his hope on a king. Fold it, set it aside with no plan to persuade anyone, and sit with the wish.

wordCard.voice: Almost persuaded. A king's half-step toward Paul's story, and Paul's answer: every good thing, and none of the chains.

orig.note: Greek: in a little. readers differ on whether Agrippa means almost, or in so short a time.

carryVoice: Your line: except these chains. A good wish, with no pressure in it. That's today, done.
